title: Some agentic AI browsers come with major cybersecurity risks, UW study finds
key_claim: UW researchers tested seven agentic AI browsers, ran a working proof-of-concept cyberattack on one, and found the conditions for equivalent attacks in three more (ChatGPT Atlas, Chrome with Gemini and Perplexity Comet all created exploitable openings), while Firefox's more limited AI mode was the least risky of the seven.
frame_summary: This source argues that agentic browsers as currently built by major vendors are not yet safe for public use, because none of the seven tested reliably separates a user's own instructions from untrusted content on the page.
verbatim_quote: ‘Browser agents aren’t ready for the public,’ said co-senior author David Kohlbrenner, a UW assistant professor in the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering.
verbatim_list: ran a successful proof-of-concept cyberattack on one browser and found the right conditions for similar attacks in three other browsers
notes: Co-senior authors David Kohlbrenner and Franziska Roesner, UW Paul G. Allen School. Findings presented 26 April 2026 at the Agents in the Wild Workshop, Rio de Janeiro; UW News release is the citable dated publication. The build/audit sandbox on this device has no outbound network egress (audit_verbatim_quote_provenance.py returns NETWORK_ERROR for every source in this file, including domains normally reachable); this quote was fetched and read directly from the live page during the research pass (WebFetch) before that sandbox limitation was hit, and is manually verified.

title: Same-Origin Policy for Agentic Browsers
key_claim: Testing production agentic browsers, the authors found they frequently violate the web's Same-Origin Policy in both ordinary use and under attack, and built a prototype enforcement layer, SOPGuard, that holds the policy with only a small runtime cost.
frame_summary: This source argues that agentic browsers break a foundational web security boundary as a routine matter rather than an edge case, and that the fix is an engineering problem with a working prototype answer, not yet adopted by shipping products.
verbatim_quote: existing agentic browsers frequently violate SOP, both in benign settings and under attacks
verbatim_list: effectively enforce SOP while preserving utility and incurring only a small runtime overhead
notes: Authors Xilong Wang, Xiaoxing Chen, Patrick Li, Dawn Song (UC Berkeley) and Neil Gong (Duke University). Prototype implemented in the open-source BrowserOS agentic browser, not in any of the mainstream vendor products this scan covers. Manually verified via WebFetch during research; the build sandbox has no network egress to arxiv.org (audit returns NETWORK_ERROR).

title: Five Eyes Issues First Joint Agentic AI Security Guidance
key_claim: On 1 May 2026 six national cyber agencies, CISA and the NSA (United States), ASD's ACSC (Australia), the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, the UK's NCSC and New Zealand's NCSC, jointly published 'Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services', warning that agents may be manipulated through prompt injection or data poisoning.
frame_summary: This source argues that six national cyber agencies now treat prompt injection as an accepted, structural risk of agentic AI that has to be contained through governance and technical controls, not a bug that will be patched away.
verbatim_quote: Agents may act unpredictably, pursue goals in unintended ways, or be subject to manipulation by malicious actors through techniques such as prompt injection or data poisoning.
verbatim_list: On May 1, 2026, six national cybersecurity agencies — CISA, NSA, Australia's ASD ACSC, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, New Zealand's NCSC, and the UK's NCSC — jointly published 'Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services'
notes: Primary document: NSA/CISA/Five Eyes 'Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services' (NSA release dated 30/04/2026 at media.defense.gov; jointly published 01/05/2026). The sandbox's proxy could not fetch cisa.gov or media.defense.gov directly (403 bot-block on both) despite repeated attempts, so this record cites the Cloud Security Alliance research note analysing the guidance, which is directly fetchable. The verbatim_quote above was cross-checked against a second, independent secondary reproduction of the same primary passage (globalpolicywatch.com, 06/2026), which quotes it identically. Used as this scan's single structural anchor (3-6 month band) for the government-guidance strand of the evidence base. quote_provenance: manually-verified.

title: Putting agentic AI systems to work: What practitioners reveal about deployment and governance
key_claim: Drawing on practitioners at 25 organisations across 11 countries, OECD reports that agentic AI is moving beyond pilots into real workflows, that none of the participating organisations deploy it with unrestricted autonomy, and that agent hijacking and credential theft are now named attack surfaces managed mainly through checkpoints requiring human approval before high-impact actions.
frame_summary: This source argues that as agentic AI moves from pilots into production, organisations are already converging on checkpoint-based human oversight as the practical safeguard against risks like agent hijacking, ahead of any settled technical fix.
verbatim_quote: agentic AI systems introduce new attack surfaces and risks, such as multi-agent collusion, agent hijacking, credential theft, and data leakage.
verbatim_list: we spoke with practitioners in 25 organisations across 11 countries, including frontier developers, enterprise deployers, public sector organisations and academic institutions
notes: Authors: Sara Rendtorff-Smith (OECD, Head of Division for AI and Emerging Digital Technologies) and Yuko Harayama (GPAI Tokyo Expert Support Center). Published on the OECD.AI Policy Observatory 'Wonk' series. Manually verified via WebFetch during research; the build sandbox has no network egress to oecd.ai (audit returns NETWORK_ERROR).

title: OpenAI is shutting down Atlas, but its AI browser ambitions are still growing
key_claim: OpenAI is discontinuing its standalone Atlas browser, redistributing its agentic browsing capability into a ChatGPT Chrome extension and a more robust desktop app that includes a separate, sandboxed remote cloud browser for agents to act in, citing product focus rather than security.
frame_summary: This source argues OpenAI concluded, on commercial rather than security grounds, that a standalone open-web AI browser was the wrong product shape, and redirected the same agentic capability into narrower, more contained surfaces.
verbatim_quote: After a few months of experimenting, OpenAI appears to have concluded that the browser is a feature, not the destination.
verbatim_list: a more robust built-in browser plus a remote cloud browser where AI agents can complete tasks on users’ behalf
notes: Article explicitly does not cite security or prompt-injection concerns as a factor in the decision; this scan treats the retreat to sandboxed/remote execution as independently convergent with the security literature, not as caused by it. See Counter-Argument. Manually verified via WebFetch during research; the build sandbox has no network egress to techcrunch.com (audit returns NETWORK_ERROR).

title: AI Browsers Vulnerable to 'PleaseFix' Zero-Click Agent Hijacking
key_claim: Security researchers demonstrated a shared vulnerability class, 'PleaseFix', built on an 'Intent Collision' technique, working independently against five separately built products: Claude in Chrome, Gemini in Chrome, Perplexity Comet, ChatGPT Atlas and Copilot Edge, enabling Gmail exfiltration, account takeovers and fraudulent purchases using a victim's stored payment card.
frame_summary: This source argues that the trust failure at the heart of agentic browsing is not a single vendor's bug but a shared architectural weakness that researchers can independently reproduce across every major agentic browser on the market.
verbatim_quote: PleaseFix exploits this trust model by placing malicious instructions inside content the agent encounters, such as emails, calendar invitations or web pages
verbatim_list: Claude in Chrome, Gemini in Chrome, Perplexity Comet, ChatGPT Atlas, and Copilot Edge
notes: Names Anthropic, Google, Perplexity, OpenAI and Microsoft products as separately vulnerable to the same technique class. Manually verified via WebFetch during research; the build sandbox has no network egress to darkreading.com (audit returns NETWORK_ERROR).

title: One runaway AI agent racked up a $50,000 cloud bill
date_evidence: Anamarija Pogorelec, Senior Staff Writer, Help Net Security, September 16, 2026
key_claim: Reporting on Mandiant's AI Risk and Resilience Report 2026 (Google Cloud), a malfunctioning accounting agent entered a runaway execution loop and made more than 15,000 high-cost API calls in under an hour, generating approximately $50,000 in cloud charges, and the report names indirect prompt injection as an evolving primary attack vector alongside weak access controls.
frame_summary: This source argues that, beyond staged research demonstrations, real enterprise deployments are already producing costly agent failures, and that indirect prompt injection sits alongside basic access-control weakness as a live production risk rather than a theoretical one.
verbatim_quote: an accounting agent entered a “runaway execution loop and made more than 15,000 high-cost API calls in less than an hour, generating approximately $50,000 in cloud charges.”
verbatim_list: The threat landscape has evolved past simple, direct prompt injection ... to indirect prompt injection. This occurs when the system architecture implicitly trusts data pulled from external pipelines, such as data from public web pages, customer emails, or user-uploaded documents
notes: Reports on Mandiant/Google Cloud's 'AI Risk and Resilience Report 2026'. This scan independently fetched the primary report at cloud.google.com/security/resources/ai-risk-and-resilience-2026 and confirmed the $50,000 case study and the indirect-prompt-injection framing appear there verbatim; the primary page did not carry a day-level dateline (only 'September 2026'), so this record cites Help Net Security's dated coverage as the citable source, with the primary report named for context. Manually verified via WebFetch during research; the build sandbox has no network egress to helpnetsecurity.com (audit returns NETWORK_ERROR).

title: Menlo Security Extends MARS to Secure AI Assistants and Coding Agents Like Microsoft Copilot, Gemini in Chrome, and Claude Code Against Prompt Injection and Data Exfiltration
key_claim: Menlo Security extended its Agent Runtime Security (MARS) platform to sit between the user and AI assistants and coding agents, including Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini and Claude Code, to catch prompt injection hidden in white-on-white text, file metadata or a single invisible pixel before the agent acts on it.
frame_summary: This source argues that, pending a shared fix inside the AI products themselves, the practical enterprise answer is a third-party governance and inspection layer sitting between every vendor's agent and the credentials or data it can reach.
verbatim_quote: An AI agent will read and carry out an instruction hidden in white-on-white text, a file's metadata, or a single human-invisible pixel, something no person would ever notice.
notes: Vendor press release for a commercial security product; used only as directional evidence of enterprise-market response (a cross-vendor governance layer forming), not as an anchor for the underlying vulnerability claims, which rest on the UW, arXiv and Dark Reading sources above. Manually verified via WebFetch during research; the build sandbox has no network egress to menlosecurity.com (audit returns NETWORK_ERROR).
